sources: Lenihan, Edmund. “The Fairies Vs. The Money Economy.” In Patricia Monaghan, ed. Irish Spirit: Pagan, Celtic, Christian, Global. Dublin: Wolfhound Press, 2001, pp. 122 ff.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The TREE was a key religious symbol for the Celts. Nearly every tree species held some magic. The THORN, or hawthorn, tied most firmly to the FAIRY world. Its spiky thorns, white blossoms, and RED haws won favor with the Good People. Some thorns marked fairy land. Thorns above old mounds, known as raths, also counted as fairy land. So did a thorn standing alone in a stony field. A set of THREE thorns also marked the land. Planted beside an OAK and an ASH, a THORN framed the grove held most sacred. Stories told of harm befalling anyone who felled a fairy tree. In the 20th century a hospital planned at Kiltimagh in Co. Mayo met such a case. The only field held two fairy trees, and no one would cut either. At last one man agreed and fell to a FAIRY STROKE on the following day. Still, the hospital went up without incident. An American-owned factory in Ulster stood over the roots of a sacrificed fairy tree. Its ruin presaged the fall of the DeLorean car company. Reverence for fairy trees endures in Ireland. In 1999 Eddie Lenihan, a schoolmaster, pushed to move a planned road so it would spare a Co. Clare fairy thorn. The Newmarket-on-Fergus thorn remains in place beside the road leading out of Shannon Airport.
